basic_information.name: Vibe Coding
basic_information.creator: Term coined by Andrej Karpathy (co-founder of OpenAI, former Senior Director of AI at Tesla). The underlying practice is enabled by multiple companies: Anysphere (Cursor), StackBlitz (Bolt.new), Lovable (formerly GPT Engineer), Replit, Vercel (v0), Anthropic (Claude Code), and others.
basic_information.release_date: February 2, 2025 — Andrej Karpathy posted on X (formerly Twitter): 'There's a new kind of coding I call vibe coding, where you fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists.' The tweet (x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383) went viral with over 4 million views. The practice itself predates the name — AI-assisted code generation tools like GitHub Copilot (launched June 2022) and Cursor (2023) had already enabled the workflow.
basic_information.license: N/A — vibe coding is a concept/practice, not a licensed product. The tools enabling it have varied licenses: Cursor (proprietary), Replit (proprietary), Bolt.new (proprietary), Claude Code (proprietary), GitHub Copilot (proprietary), with some open-source alternatives emerging.
basic_information.current_version: N/A — as a concept, vibe coding has no version. The term was added to Merriam-Webster as a 'slang & trending' entry in March 2025, and Collins Dictionary named it Word of the Year 2025 in November 2025. The practice continues to evolve rapidly as underlying LLMs improve.

technical_architecture.architecture_pattern: N/A — vibe coding is a development practice, not a technical architecture. It encompasses multiple patterns: code_first (Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code), pipeline (Bolt.new, Lovable), and single_agent or multi_agent systems depending on the tool. The common denominator is natural language input producing executable code, with the human acting as project director rather than code author.
technical_architecture.underlying_models: Vibe coding tools leverage frontier LLMs: Claude 3.5/4 Sonnet and Opus (Anthropic, used by Cursor and Claude Code), GPT-4o/o1/o3 (OpenAI, used by Copilot and various tools), Gemini 2.5 Pro (Google, used by Replit and Jules), and proprietary fine-tuned models. Claude Sonnet models are widely considered the best for code generation as of early 2026. Cursor specifically rose to prominence using 'Cursor Composer w Sonnet' as Karpathy noted in his original tweet.
technical_architecture.tool_integration: Varies by tool. IDE-based tools (Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot) integrate via editor extensions with file system access, terminal execution, and MCP server connections. Web-based tools (Bolt.new, Lovable, Replit) provide integrated preview, deployment, and database provisioning. All tools support some form of context injection — codebases, documentation, error messages. Claude Code supports MCP natively. The key interaction pattern is: human describes intent in natural language → LLM generates code → tool executes/previews → human evaluates output visually → iterates.
technical_architecture.planning_approach: code_as_plan — the defining characteristic of vibe coding is that the LLM handles planning, architecture, and implementation simultaneously. The human provides high-level goals and constraints; the AI decomposes tasks and generates code. More advanced tools (Claude Code, Cursor Agent mode, Replit Agent) use ReAct-style planning with tool use: plan → write code → execute → observe errors → fix → iterate. Simpler tools (Bolt.new, Lovable) use single-shot or multi-turn generation with preview feedback.
technical_architecture.multi_agent_support: Emerging. Most current vibe coding tools use a single agent model, but multi-agent approaches are appearing: Replit Agent orchestrates multiple sub-agents for different tasks (frontend, backend, database), Cursor supports agent mode with autonomous tool use, and Claude Code can spawn sub-agents. The trend is toward more autonomous multi-agent systems that handle full-stack development.

memory_and_context.memory_types_supported: short_term (conversation context within a session), semantic (codebase indexing via embeddings). IDE-based tools (Cursor, Windsurf) index the full codebase for semantic retrieval. Web-based tools (Bolt.new, Lovable) maintain project state within the session. Long-term memory across sessions varies — Cursor maintains project-level context through .cursorrules files, Claude Code uses CLAUDE.md files, and Replit persists full project state.
memory_and_context.context_window_management: Critical challenge for vibe coding. Tools use various strategies: codebase indexing with retrieval (Cursor, Windsurf), file-level context selection (Claude Code), full-project inclusion for smaller projects (Bolt.new), and RAG-based approaches. The quality of context management directly impacts code generation quality. Cursor and Claude Code allow users to @-mention specific files to control context. Token limits of underlying models (128K-200K+ tokens) constrain how much code context can be included.
memory_and_context.persistence_mechanism: file_system (IDE tools write directly to the user's project), cloud (web-based tools like Replit, Lovable persist projects on their platforms), in_memory (conversation state). Project configuration persists via convention files: .cursorrules (Cursor), CLAUDE.md (Claude Code), .replit (Replit).
memory_and_context.context_engineering_approach: Context is increasingly treated as a first-class concern. Best practices emerging in the vibe coding community include: structured project descriptions, rules files (.cursorrules, CLAUDE.md) that encode project conventions, explicit file references in prompts, and error message copy-paste (as Karpathy described: 'if it doesn't work, I just copy the error message back'). The quality of natural language instructions directly determines output quality — a key skill gap for non-technical users.

capabilities.core_capabilities: DEFINITION: Vibe coding is an AI-assisted software development practice where a person describes a project or task in natural language to an LLM, which generates source code. The practitioner does not write or review code directly but instead evaluates output through execution and visual inspection, providing feedback iteratively. KEY CAPABILITIES ACROSS TOOLS: (1) NATURAL LANGUAGE TO CODE: Describe features, UI elements, logic in plain English (or any language) and receive working code. (2) FULL-STACK GENERATION: Frontend (React, Next.js, HTML/CSS), backend (Node.js, Python, APIs), database schemas, and deployment configuration. (3) ITERATIVE REFINEMENT: 'See stuff, say stuff, run stuff, copy-paste stuff' (Karpathy). Error messages are fed back to the AI for debugging. (4) RAPID PROTOTYPING: Working prototypes in minutes to hours — Bolt.new averages 28 minutes to working prototype, Lovable 35 minutes. (5) VOICE-DRIVEN DEVELOPMENT: Karpathy used SuperWhisper to dictate to Cursor, enabling fully hands-free coding. (6) DEPLOYMENT: Several tools (Lovable, Replit, Bolt.new) offer one-click deployment to production. (7) ACCESSIBILITY: Enables non-developers (CEOs, marketers, designers) to build functional software — Andrew Ng reports his CFO, general counsel, and receptionist all code at AI Fund.
capabilities.supported_modalities: Text (natural language prompts), code (generation and editing), vision (screenshot-to-code in some tools like v0, Lovable), browser (web preview and testing), file_system (IDE tools), voice (via SuperWhisper or similar dictation tools). Multimodal inputs (uploading designs, wireframes) are supported by v0, Lovable, and Bolt.new.
capabilities.autonomy_level: Ranges from copilot to fully_autonomous depending on tool and use case. Karpathy's original definition is essentially fully_autonomous: 'forget that the code even exists' and 'always accept all' changes. In practice, most usage is copilot (Cursor, Copilot) or assistant (Bolt.new, Lovable, Replit Agent) with the human providing goals and evaluating outputs. The trend is toward greater autonomy — Replit Agent and Claude Code can execute multi-step tasks with minimal intervention.
capabilities.tool_ecosystem: MAJOR VIBE CODING TOOLS (as of early 2026): IDE-based: Cursor ($29.3B valuation, $1B+ ARR), GitHub Copilot (1.8M+ paid subscribers), Windsurf (Codeium), Claude Code (Anthropic). Web-based/No-code: Lovable ($6.6B valuation, $200M+ ARR), Bolt.new (StackBlitz, ~$40M+ ARR), Replit ($3B valuation, $250M ARR), v0 (Vercel), Anything ($100M valuation in 2 weeks). Specialized: Devin (Cognition Labs, autonomous software engineer), Google Jules, OpenAI Codex CLI.

agent_interoperability.mcp_support: Supported by Claude Code natively. Cursor added MCP support in 2025. Other tools have varying levels of MCP integration. MCP enables vibe coding tools to connect to external data sources, APIs, and services through a standardized protocol, expanding what can be built through natural language.
agent_interoperability.a2a_support: Limited direct A2A support in current vibe coding tools. Multi-agent orchestration is emerging but mostly within single platforms (Replit Agent sub-agents, Claude Code sub-agents) rather than cross-platform agent-to-agent communication.
agent_interoperability.agents_md_support: Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md project instructions. Cursor reads .cursorrules. These serve a similar purpose to AGENTS.md — encoding project conventions, coding standards, and constraints that guide AI behavior. The practice of maintaining instruction files is becoming standard in vibe coding workflows.
agent_interoperability.cross_framework_compatibility: Moderate. Code generated by vibe coding tools is standard code (React, Python, etc.) that works in any environment. However, project configurations and tool-specific settings don't transfer between platforms. A project started in Cursor can be continued in Claude Code (both work on local files), but moving from Lovable to Cursor requires exporting and restructuring.

safety_and_guardrails.permission_model: Varies widely. IDE-based tools (Cursor, Claude Code) operate within the user's local environment with full file system access — Claude Code has an explicit allow/deny permission model for commands. Web-based tools (Bolt.new, Lovable) run in sandboxed environments with more restricted access. A critical concern: vibe coding users often grant broad permissions without understanding implications because they don't review the generated code.
safety_and_guardrails.escalation_policy: Minimal in most tools. IDE tools show diffs that users can accept/reject, but Karpathy's definition explicitly involves 'always accepting all changes.' Web-based tools show preview results. The fundamental safety concern: vibe coders by definition do not review code, so escalation based on code-level concerns is absent. Some tools (Claude Code) refuse certain dangerous operations and ask for confirmation.
safety_and_guardrails.hallucination_mitigation: A major concern. 45% of AI-generated code contains security vulnerabilities (multiple studies, 2025). AI models hallucinate non-existent package dependency names, which can be exploited for supply chain attacks. OWASP Top-10 vulnerabilities appear in 45% of vibe-coded output even when code compiles successfully 90% of the time. Mitigation strategies: some tools include automated testing, linting, and type-checking. Lovable had a 'VibeScamming' vulnerability discovered by Guardio Labs (April 2025) where prompt injection could create backdoors.
safety_and_guardrails.audit_trail: Limited. IDE-based tools rely on git version control for audit trails. Web-based tools maintain project history but with varying granularity. The rapid, iterative nature of vibe coding ('accept all changes') means git histories can be opaque — commits may contain large AI-generated changesets without meaningful messages.
safety_and_guardrails.human_oversight_pattern: The defining tension of vibe coding. Karpathy's original concept explicitly minimizes oversight: 'forget that the code even exists.' In practice: (1) PROTOTYPE MODE: minimal oversight, accept all, iterate by visual inspection. (2) PRODUCTION MODE: requires code review, testing, security scanning — at which point it transitions from 'vibe coding' to 'AI-assisted development.' Andrew Ng argues this is 'a deeply intellectual exercise' even without reading code. The industry is split: 63% of developers report spending more time debugging AI-generated code than writing it would have taken, at least once.

governance_and_standards.governance_body: No formal governance body for vibe coding as a practice. Relevant standards organizations: OWASP (developing security guidelines for AI-generated code), ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42 (AI standards), EU AI Act (regulatory framework). The Linux Foundation and CNCF are developing guidelines for AI-assisted software supply chain security.
governance_and_standards.contributing_protocols: No protocols specific to vibe coding. The practice benefits from: MCP (expanding tool integration), function calling standards (enabling tool use), and emerging code quality standards for AI-generated output. SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) standards are increasingly relevant as AI-generated dependencies need tracking.
governance_and_standards.regulatory_compliance: Emerging concern. EU_AI_Act implications: code generated by AI that powers high-risk systems may require disclosure and audit trails. No specific regulations yet for vibe-coded software, but the practice raises questions about: (1) liability for AI-generated bugs and security flaws, (2) intellectual property ownership of AI-generated code, (3) compliance with software engineering standards in regulated industries (medical devices, financial services, aviation). 53-62% of organizations cite security and compliance concerns with AI-generated code.

deployment_and_operations.deployment_modes: cloud (Lovable, Bolt.new, Replit provide integrated cloud deployment), local (IDE tools generate code that deploys anywhere), hybrid (code generated locally, deployed to cloud). Web-based vibe coding tools increasingly offer one-click deployment to Vercel, Netlify, or their own hosting. Replit provides integrated hosting for all generated applications.
deployment_and_operations.scalability_model: N/A for vibe coding as a concept. The scalability of vibe-coded applications depends entirely on the generated architecture. A key criticism: vibe-coded applications often lack proper scalability considerations. 'The code often works just well enough to pass initial tests, but tends to be brittle and poorly organized under the hood.' For tools themselves: Cursor and Copilot scale horizontally via cloud LLM APIs; web-based tools use serverless architectures.
deployment_and_operations.cost_per_task: TOOL PRICING: Cursor Pro $20/month (500 fast requests), Cursor Business $40/month; GitHub Copilot $10-39/month; Lovable free tier + $20-65/month paid; Bolt.new free tier + $20-200/month; Replit free tier + $25-220/month; Claude Code via API usage (~$5-50 per coding session depending on complexity). UNDERLYING COSTS: LLM API costs per generation range from $0.01-$2.00 depending on model and context size. Cursor reported $1B ARR suggesting average user spend ~$17-20/month. PRODUCTIVITY VALUE: McKinsey reports 20-50% faster development for code generation and refactoring tasks.
deployment_and_operations.resource_requirements: For users: a modern web browser (web-based tools) or VS Code-compatible editor (Cursor, Windsurf). No specialized hardware required — all LLM inference happens in the cloud. Internet connection required. For non-trivial projects: familiarity with version control (git), basic understanding of web technologies (for web apps), and ability to articulate requirements clearly in natural language. Karpathy used SuperWhisper (voice-to-text) plus Cursor on a standard laptop.

observability_and_ops.monitoring_integration: N/A for vibe coding as a practice. The tools themselves have varying monitoring: Cursor tracks usage and rate limits, web-based tools provide project dashboards. For vibe-coded applications, monitoring is typically not included unless explicitly requested — a significant gap. Some tools (Replit) auto-include basic error tracking.
observability_and_ops.tracing_support: Limited. IDE tools (Cursor, Claude Code) show conversation history and can replay prompts. Web-based tools maintain generation history. However, understanding why AI generated specific code requires re-reading conversation context. The 'accept all' mindset of vibe coding means trace-back debugging is difficult — vibe-coded applications generate longer code than human-written equivalents, making debugging 'tedious or even futile.'
observability_and_ops.production_readiness_level: The practice itself is experimental to beta for production use. Consensus view: vibe coding is production_ready for prototypes, MVPs, and internal tools; experimental for customer-facing production software. The Wall Street Journal reported in July 2025 that professional engineers were adopting it for commercial use cases, but Fast Company reported the 'vibe coding hangover' in September 2025 with engineers citing 'development hell.' Gartner predicts 40% of new production software will use vibe coding techniques by 2028.

adoption_and_market.github_stars: N/A — vibe coding is a practice, not a single repository. Key tool GitHub metrics: Cursor (closed source, no public repo), Bolt.new/oTToDev fork ~30K+ stars, Lovable (closed source), Replit (various open-source projects). The concept itself has a Wikipedia article and Wiktionary entry.
adoption_and_market.adoption_scale: DEVELOPER ADOPTION: 85% of developers regularly using AI coding tools by late 2025. 92% of US developers using AI coding tools daily. 41% of all code is AI-generated (GitHub, 2025). Y Combinator W25 batch: 25% of startups had codebases 95% AI-generated. TOOL-SPECIFIC: Cursor >1M users, 720K paying ($1B ARR), fastest SaaS to $500M ARR ever. Lovable $200M+ ARR in 12 months, $6.6B valuation. Replit $250M ARR, $3B valuation, expects $1B ARR by end 2026. Bolt.new $40M+ ARR within 5 months of launch. Combined leading startup valuations grew 350% YoY to $36B+ in 2025, generating ~$800M collective ARR. ENTERPRISE: Gartner forecasts 60% of new software code will be AI-generated by 2026. 90% of Fortune 100 companies using AI development tools. CULTURAL IMPACT: Collins Dictionary Word of the Year 2025. Merriam-Webster slang entry (March 2025). Linus Torvalds publicly vibe-coded a Python tool component (January 2026).
adoption_and_market.pricing_model: Freemium is the dominant model. All major tools offer free tiers with usage limits and paid tiers ($10-220/month) for increased capacity. Enterprise pricing available for Cursor, Copilot, and Replit. API-based pricing for Claude Code. The market is intensely competitive with pricing pressure — tools compete on free tier generosity and model quality.
adoption_and_market.key_use_cases: PRIMARY: (1) Rapid prototyping and MVP development (the canonical use case), (2) Internal tools and automation for non-engineering teams, (3) Frontend/UI development from descriptions or screenshots, (4) Startup product development (25% of YC W25 batch), (5) Personal projects and side projects, (6) Learning to code and educational use (Andrew Ng's Vibe Coding 101 course with Replit). EMERGING: (7) Enterprise application development (Wall Street Journal, July 2025), (8) Non-developer software creation (CEOs, marketers, designers building tools), (9) Game development and creative coding. INDUSTRIES: Technology/startups (dominant), education, marketing/creative, finance (internal tools), healthcare (prototyping).
adoption_and_market.competitive_position: Vibe coding sits at the intersection of multiple markets: AI coding assistants ($22B+ market), no-code/low-code platforms ($65B+ market by 2027), and software development tools. KEY COMPETITIVE DYNAMICS: IDE-based tools (Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf) compete on developer experience and code quality for professional developers. Web-based tools (Lovable, Bolt.new, Replit) compete on accessibility for non-developers and speed-to-deployment. The market is consolidating: OpenAI acquired Windsurf (Codeium) for $3B in 2025. Cursor leads in revenue and valuation ($29.3B). The practice threatens traditional no-code platforms (Bubble, Webflow) and potentially reduces demand for junior developers.

ecosystem_maturity.community_size: Massive and rapidly growing. The vibe coding community spans: Reddit (r/vibecoding, r/cursor, r/ChatGPTCoding with hundreds of thousands of members), X/Twitter (the term trends regularly), YouTube (thousands of tutorials), Discord communities for each major tool. The broader AI-assisted coding community includes millions of developers globally. Cursor alone has 1M+ users. The concept has mainstream cultural awareness — Collins Word of the Year 2025.
ecosystem_maturity.documentation_quality: good — major tools (Cursor, Replit, Lovable) have comprehensive documentation. The practice itself is well-documented through blog posts, tutorials, and courses. Andrew Ng and DeepLearning.AI launched 'Vibe Coding 101 with Replit' course. Google Cloud and IBM published official explainers. Academic research is emerging (Andy Gordon's paper 'Vibe coding: programming through conversation with artificial intelligence'). However, the field evolves so rapidly that documentation can become outdated within months.
ecosystem_maturity.third_party_integrations_count: Hundreds across the ecosystem. Cursor supports MCP servers (100+), GitHub Copilot integrates with the entire GitHub ecosystem, Replit supports dozens of frameworks and deployment targets, Lovable connects to Supabase, Stripe, and various APIs. The integration landscape is expanding rapidly as MCP adoption grows.
ecosystem_maturity.tutorial_availability: Excellent. Resources include: Andrew Ng's DeepLearning.AI Vibe Coding 101 course, Google Cloud's official guide, IBM's explainer, thousands of YouTube tutorials (Build with AI, Fireship, etc.), Medium and Dev.to articles, university courses incorporating vibe coding, and dedicated learning platforms. Most tool vendors provide extensive onboarding tutorials.

human_agent_interaction.autonomy_spectrum: Spans the full range depending on tool and user. Original Karpathy definition: fully_delegated ('forget that the code even exists, always accept all changes'). Common practice for prototyping: autonomous (minimal code review). Recommended for production: assistant (executes with approval, code reviewed). Andrew Ng's perspective: copilot ('a deeply intellectual exercise'). The spectrum is shifting toward greater autonomy as models improve — Replit Agent and Claude Code handle multi-step tasks with decreasing human intervention.
human_agent_interaction.handoff_mechanism: In vibe coding, handoff occurs at the output level rather than the code level: (1) The human evaluates the running application visually, (2) Errors or unwanted behavior trigger another prompt to the AI, (3) For production deployment, vibe-coded prototypes are typically handed to professional developers for review, refactoring, and hardening. Some tools (Cursor, Claude Code) support explicit handoff by generating documentation or TODO comments for human follow-up.
human_agent_interaction.feedback_loop: The core feedback loop in vibe coding is: describe → generate → execute → observe → refine. This happens in real-time within a single session. Cross-session learning varies: Cursor and Claude Code learn project conventions through rules files (.cursorrules, CLAUDE.md). LLM providers improve models based on aggregate usage patterns. User satisfaction feedback (thumbs up/down) in some tools influences model fine-tuning. The key insight: the feedback is on outputs (does the app work?) rather than on code quality — which is both the appeal and the risk.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: CRITICAL for M2 Entrepreneurship students. Key insights: (1) DEMOCRATIZATION: Vibe coding radically lowers the barrier to building software. Andrew Ng: 'The bar to coding is now lower than it ever has been.' Non-technical founders can now build functional MVPs without a technical co-founder — 25% of YC W25 startups had 95% AI-generated codebases. (2) SPEED TO MARKET: Prototypes in hours, not weeks. Lovable: 35 min to working prototype. This enables rapid hypothesis testing and customer validation. (3) COST REDUCTION: Solo founders can build what previously required a 3-5 person engineering team. Tools cost $20-65/month vs. $10K+/month for engineers. (4) INVESTMENT LANDSCAPE: Vibe coding startups raised massive funding in 2025 — Cursor ($2.3B), Lovable ($500M+), Replit ($250M). VCs are actively funding this category. (5) WHEN TO USE: Prototyping, MVPs, internal tools, marketing sites, simple web apps. (6) WHEN TO AVOID: Security-critical systems, regulated industries (medical, financial), applications requiring high reliability, complex system architecture. (7) RISKS: 45% of AI-generated code has security vulnerabilities. Technical debt accumulates fast. 63% of developers spent more time debugging than writing would have taken. The 'vibe coding hangover' is real. (8) STRATEGIC ADVICE: Use vibe coding to validate business hypotheses cheaply and quickly, then invest in proper engineering for products that gain traction. 'Prototype with vibes, ship with engineers.'
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy: For non-technical startup founders: START with web-based vibe coding tools (Lovable, Bolt.new, Replit) for initial prototyping — $0-65/month, no setup required. UPGRADE to IDE-based tools (Cursor) when projects grow complex and you hire developers. BUY hosted infrastructure (Vercel, Supabase, Stripe) rather than building from scratch. HIRE professional developers for production hardening of successful prototypes. Key decision framework: If your MVP is a web app or internal tool, vibe code it. If it's a complex system with security requirements, hire engineers from day one. The tools pay for themselves if they save even one week of development time. CAUTION: Don't confuse a working prototype with a production-ready product — the gap is significant and often underestimated.
entrepreneurial_relevance.session_mapping: Session 2 (Prompt Engineering & No-Code Tools) — vibe coding as the evolution of prompt engineering from text generation to software generation; comparison with no-code tools. Session 3 (Framing & Managing AI Projects) — vibe coding's role in rapid prototyping within CRISP-DM, build-vs-buy decisions. Session 5 (Ethics, Governance & Final Presentations) — security risks, IP questions, liability for AI-generated code.

confidence.data_quality: High — vibe coding is extensively covered by major publications (Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg, CNN, TechCrunch, Forbes), research firms (Gartner, McKinsey), major tech companies (IBM, Google Cloud published official explainers), and academic research. Financial data (ARR, valuations) comes from authoritative sources (TechCrunch, CNBC, Bloomberg, Sacra). The Wikipedia article is well-sourced. Collins Dictionary Word of the Year adds cultural validation. Data recency: most sources from 2025-early 2026.
confidence.cross_reference: Multiple independent sources confirm: (1) Karpathy's February 2025 origin: confirmed by X post, Wikipedia, IBM, Google Cloud, all major publications. (2) Adoption statistics: GitHub (41% AI-generated code), Stack Overflow surveys, Gartner forecasts, Y Combinator data — all align on massive adoption. (3) Revenue/valuation data: Cursor $29.3B / $1B ARR (TechCrunch, Bloomberg, SaaStr), Lovable $6.6B / $200M ARR (TechCrunch, CNBC, Bloomberg), Replit $3B / $250M ARR (TechCrunch, Replit press release) — consistent across sources. (4) Security concerns: 45% vulnerability rate confirmed by multiple independent studies (InfoWorld, CSO Online, Databricks, Kaspersky, OWASP). (5) Collins Word of the Year: confirmed by CNN, Euronews, Collins official site.
confidence.caveats: KEY CAVEATS: (1) RAPIDLY EVOLVING: The vibe coding landscape changes weekly. New tools launch constantly, existing tools add features, and underlying models improve. Data from even 3 months ago may be outdated. (2) MARKET SIZE ESTIMATES VARY: 'Vibe coding market' estimates range wildly ($2.96B to $3.89B for 2024-2025) because there's no agreed definition of what constitutes the 'vibe coding market' vs. the broader AI coding assistant market. (3) HYPE CYCLE: The practice may be at or near peak hype. Fast Company's 'vibe coding hangover' article (September 2025) suggests a correction is underway. 63% of developers found debugging AI code harder than expected. (4) SURVIVORSHIP BIAS: Success stories (Lovable, Cursor) are highly visible; failures are not. The 40% Gartner cancellation rate for agentic AI projects likely applies to vibe-coded projects too. (5) SECURITY DEBT: The 45% vulnerability rate is well-documented but the long-term implications of widespread vibe-coded software in production are unknown. (6) DEFINITION DRIFT: 'Vibe coding' now means different things to different people — from Karpathy's extreme version (never read code) to any AI-assisted development. Andrew Ng explicitly pushed back on the term, calling it 'a bad name for a real and exhausting job.' (7) NON-DEVELOPER LIMITATION: While the promise is democratization, non-developers still face significant challenges with debugging, architecture decisions, and deployment — the tools work best for simple applications.
